notes.subtopic: 1. Big Picture — From Medieval to Modern
notes.content:
**Executive summary:** History is divided into **ancient, medieval and modern** periods. Europe's **medieval period (Middle Ages)** lasted from the **5th to the 15th century**. From the early **14th to the late 16th century**, the **Renaissance** and the **Age of Discovery** mark Europe's transition to the **Modern Age**. From **1750**, the **Industrial Revolution** transformed Western societies.

**Chapter map:** Sources → Renaissance → Age of Discovery → Reformation → Counter Reformation → Industrial Revolution → Imperialism.

**Primary vs secondary sources**
| Primary sources | Secondary sources |
|---|---|
| First-hand, original evidence from the past | Derived by interpreting and analysing primary sources |
| Oral histories, objects, artefacts, photographs, newspapers, census records, diaries, journals, inventories | Most history books in a library; **your history textbook** |

fiveW.who: Greek scholars, merchant-nobles, Gutenberg, thinkers like Petrarca
fiveW.where: Began in Florence (Italy), spread across Europe
fiveW.what: 'Rebirth' — a cultural movement in art, literature, science and thought
fiveW.why: Fall of Constantinople, new wealthy patrons, new routes, Crusades, printing press
fiveW.how: Scholars and printed books spread new ideas; people began to question old beliefs

notes.content:
**Renaissance** = cultural movement that began in **Florence (Italy)** in the late Middle Ages; influenced literature, philosophy, art, politics, science and religion.

**Causes — remember 'FRDCP'**
• **F**all of Constantinople (**1453**) — Ottoman Turks captured this centre of learning; Greek scholars fled to **Italy** → Florence, Venice, Milan became centres of education.
• **R**ise of a new nobility — rich **merchants** (not nobles by birth) **patronised learning**.
• **D**iscovery of new routes — trade hampered after 1453 → new routes and lands → new centres of trade and **cultural exchange**.
• **C**rusades — Holy Wars brought Europe into contact with the **Arabs**, advanced in science and philosophy.
• **P**rinting press — **Johannes Gutenberg**; spread ideas; translations of the Bible made people question old practices.

**Features**
• **Humanism** — focus shifted from God to **human life**; **Francesco Petrarca = 'Father of Humanism'**.
• **Rationalism** — everything has a reason; right to question, even the Church.
• **Scientific spirit** — observation → experimentation → conclusion.
• **Spirit of inquiry** (most important) — led to voyages and discovery of new lands.
• **Realism** — art showed real beauty of the world and people.

**Impact on literature:** Latin discarded; writing in **local languages**.
| Scholar | Work |
|---|---|
| Dante | The Divine Comedy |
| Machiavelli | The Prince |
| Erasmus | The Praise of Folly |
| Shakespeare | Julius Caesar, The Merchant of Venice, Macbeth |
| John Milton | Paradise Lost |
| Geoffrey Chaucer | The Canterbury Tales |

**Art:** Florence produced **Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Raphael**; themes moved from religious to secular; realistic human anatomy.
**Sculpture:** Michelangelo's **Pieta** (Rome).
**Architecture:** rounded arches, domes, tall Grecian pillars — **Graeco-Roman style**.

notes.content:
**Motives:** wealth (gold, silver, spices) · power in Europe · trade · spreading Christianity · building empires.

| Explorer | Achievement |
|---|---|
| Bartolomeu Dias | First European to sail round the **Cape of Good Hope** |
| Christopher Columbus | Discovered the **New World (America)** |
| Vasco da Gama | **Sea route from Portugal to the East** (India) |

**Comparative history:** **Inca Empire** (Ecuador, Chile, Peru, Argentina, Bolivia) — largest empire in early 16th century; **Machu Picchu**. **Aztec Empire** (Mexico) — capital **Tenochtitlan**, captured by the Spanish in **1521**.

fiveW.who: Martin Luther (Germany); also Zwingli, Calvin, Henry VIII
fiveW.where: Began in Wittenberg, Germany; spread to Switzerland, France, England
fiveW.what: Protestant movement to reform the Catholic Church
fiveW.why: Corruption in the Church and clergy; authority of the pope questioned
fiveW.how: Theses posted on the church door; Bible translated into German; pamphlets for common people

notes.content:
**Reformation** = 16th-century religious, political, intellectual and cultural upheaval — an attempt by **Protestants to reform the Catholic Church**. One of the greatest events in world history.

**Dating:** begins **1517** (Luther's **Ninety-five Theses**) · ends **1555** (**Peace of Augsburg** — Lutheran and Catholic churches coexist in Germany).

**Martin Luther (1483–1546)**
• Taught at the **University of Wittenberg**; appalled by Church corruption.
• **1517** — posted the Ninety-five Theses on the castle church door, Wittenberg.
• **1521** — summoned before the **Diet of Worms** and **excommunicated**.
• Helped by the ruler of **Saxony**, translated the **Bible into German**.
• **1524** — German peasants revolted.

**Spread:** Switzerland — **Ulrich Zwingli**; France — **John Calvin**; England — **King Henry VIII**.

notes.subtopic: 6. Counter Reformation and Impact of the Reformation

fiveW.who: Roman Catholic Church; Ignatius of Loyola (Jesuits)
fiveW.when: Council of Trent from 1545; Society of Jesus 1534
fiveW.why: To stop the spread of Protestantism and remove abuses
fiveW.how: Reforms of the Council of Trent and preaching by the Jesuits

notes.content:
**Council of Trent (1545) reforms**
• New edition of the **Latin Bible**; heretical books banned.
• **Sale of church offices prohibited**; no fee for religious ceremonies.
• Clergy to lead a **moral life**.
• **Society of Jesus (Jesuits)** founded by **Ignatius of Loyola** (1534).
• By the end of the 16th century the Church regained people's faith; Europe split into **Catholics and Protestants**.

**Impact of the Reformation**
• Broke barriers of class and education; old religious values set aside.
• **King/government, not the Church, ruled the state**.
• Science flourished.
• **Individual liberty** — follow one's own conscience.
• **National churches → nation states** with power in the king's hands.
• Decline of feudalism; **banking, finance, new trade** → economic growth.

fiveW.who: British landlords, inventors (Kay, Hargreaves, Watt…), entrepreneurs
fiveW.what: Shift from an agriculture-based to a manufacturing-based economy
fiveW.why: Enclosures, coal and iron, colonies as markets, stable government, rich middle class, inventions
fiveW.how: Machines powered by fossil fuels, factories, mass production, mechanised transport

notes.content:
**Term popularised by Arnold Toynbee** (British economic historian) for Britain's development **1760–1840**.

**Why Britain? (7 reasons)**
• **Enclosure Movement** — Acts of Parliament let landlords buy and enclose small strips → machines used → more production (*agricultural revolution led to industrial revolution*).
• Plenty of **coal and iron**.
• **Transport** — James Watt's steam engine.
• **Vast overseas market** — colonies in India and Africa.
• **Stable government**.
• **Prosperous middle class** of entrepreneurs.
• **New inventions**.

| Invention | Inventor | Year |
|---|---|---|
| Flying shuttle | John Kay | 1733 |
| Spinning jenny | James Hargreaves | 1764 |
| Steam engine | James Watt | 1769 |
| Spinning mule | Samuel Crompton | 1779 |
| Power loom | Edmund Cartwright | 1785 |
| Cotton gin | Eli Whitney | 1793 |

• Production increased manifold; **domestic system → factory system**.
• **Urbanisation** — new social classes and divisions.
• Poor working conditions → workers demanded rights; **Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels** → rise of **socialism**.
• Dramatic **increase in population**; migration from villages to cities.
• Improved agriculture reduced **famines**.

**Analogy (textbook):** machines : increased production :: industrialisation : urbanisation :: social revolution : **socialism**.

**Imperialism** = one country's domination of the political, economic and social life of another; today it means **Western control over Asia and Africa**.

**Forms**
• **Colony** — ruled directly through colonial officials.
• **Protectorate** — own government, but policies guided by a foreign power.
• **Sphere of influence** — region where the imperial power had **exclusive trading rights**.

**Causes**
• Industrial Revolution → demand for **raw materials, markets, cheap labour** → strong military to protect interests.
• **Nationalist rivalry** — scramble for colonies.
• **Religious fervour** and feelings of **racial and cultural superiority**.

• **India:** British defeated the French in **1760**; expanded through wars, diplomacy and trade.
• **Burma:** inroads in the **1820s**; full control over the next 60 years.
• **Maldives:** British **protectorate 1887–1965** (on trade routes).
• **Ceylon (Sri Lanka):** Portuguese → Dutch (**1658**) → British (**1796**) → official British colony **1802**.

| Positive impact | Negative impact |
|---|---|
| Christian missionary activity | Colonies = cheap raw materials |
| Western education | Colonies exploited for the rulers' prosperity |
| Technology — weapons, medicines, farming | Welfare of colonies ignored |
| Learnt about new governments, organisation | Trade monopolised |
| **Nationalism → freedom struggles** | Rivalry → **World Wars I and II** |

questions.question: What were the causes of the Renaissance?
questions.answer:
• Fall of Constantinople (1453): Ottoman Turks captured it; Greek scholars fled to Italy, making Florence, Venice and Milan centres of learning.
  • Rise of a new nobility: rich merchants patronised learning.
  • Discovery of new routes: new trade centres became sites of cultural exchange.
  • Crusades: contact with the Arabs, advanced in science and philosophy.
  • Printing press (Gutenberg): spread ideas; translated Bible made people question old beliefs.
questions.topperTip: Mnemonic FRDCP — Fall, Rise, Discovery, Crusades, Printing.

questions.question: Describe the characteristics (features) of the Renaissance.
questions.answer:
• Humanism: focus shifted from God to human life; Petrarca — 'Father of Humanism'.
  • Rationalism: everything has a reason; people questioned even the Church.
  • Scientific spirit: observation, experimentation, conclusion.
  • Spirit of inquiry: the most important feature; led to voyages of discovery.
  • Realism: art showed the real beauty of the world and of people.

questions.question: How did the invention of the printing press impact the Renaissance? (Picture: Gutenberg)
questions.answer:
• (a) Johannes Gutenberg. (b) He invented the printing press.
  • (c) Books became cheap and plentiful, so ideas spread quickly across Europe; translations of the Bible and other works made people aware, and they began to question age-old practices and beliefs.

questions.question: How did the fall of Constantinople result in the discovery of new sea routes? What motivated the explorers?
questions.answer:
• After 1453 the Turks controlled the land and sea routes to the East, so trade was hampered; Europeans searched for new sea routes to keep trade profitable.
  • Motives: wealth (gold, silver, spices), power in Europe, trade, spreading Christianity and building empires; aided by the mariner's compass and adjustable sails.

questions.question: Why is the Reformation of the 16th century regarded as one of the greatest events in world history?
questions.answer:
• It broke barriers of class and education and set aside old religious values.
  • The king/government, not the Church, now ruled the state.
  • Science flourished.
  • It gave the true meaning of individual liberty — following one's own conscience.
  • It asserted the sovereignty of nations; national churches led to the rise of nation states.
  • Decline of feudalism; banking, finance and trade led to economic growth.
questions.topperTip: Group the points under Political / Religious / Economic headings for a long answer.

questions.question: Who was Martin Luther? Explain his contribution to the Reformation.
questions.answer:
• German monk and professor at the University of Wittenberg (1483–1546), appalled by Church corruption.
  • 1517: posted the Ninety-five Theses on the castle church door at Wittenberg — beginning of the Reformation.
  • 1521: excommunicated at the Diet of Worms.
  • Translated the Bible into German and spread pamphlets for common people; Lutheran churches were established all over Germany.

questions.question: What was the Counter Reformation? State the reforms of the Council of Trent.
questions.answer:
The Catholic Church's response to Luther and the Protestants.

  • Council of Trent (1545): new Latin Bible; heretical books banned; sale of church offices prohibited; no fees for ceremonies; clergy to lead a moral life.
  • Jesuits (Society of Jesus, Ignatius of Loyola, 1534) worked to restore faith — by the end of the 16th century the Church regained people's faith.

questions.question: Why did the Industrial Revolution begin in Britain?
questions.answer:
• Enclosure Movement: landlords enclosed small strips; machines raised farm output.
  • Coal and iron in plenty.
  • Transport: James Watt's steam engine.
  • Vast overseas market: colonies in India and Africa.
  • Stable government and a prosperous middle class that invested in factories.
  • New inventions — flying shuttle, spinning jenny, power loom.
questions.topperTip: Write 'agricultural revolution led to the industrial revolution' — examiners love this line.

questions.question: How did the Industrial Revolution change the social and economic structure of Britain?
questions.answer:
• Economic: production increased manifold; domestic system gave way to the factory system; agriculture improved, reducing famines.
  • Social: urbanisation with new classes and divisions; people moved from villages to cities; population rose sharply.
  • Poor working conditions → workers demanded rights → Marx and Engels → socialism.

questions.question: What were the main factors for the rise of imperialism in the 1800s?
questions.answer:
• The Industrial Revolution created demand for raw materials, new markets and cheap labour.
  • A strong military was needed to protect economic interests.
  • Nationalist rivalry — European nations scrambled for colonies.
  • Religious fervour and a sense of racial and cultural superiority.

questions.question: 'The Industrial Revolution gave rise to imperialism, which led to the exploitation of the colonies.' Do you support the statement?
questions.answer:
Yes.

  • Factories needed raw materials and markets — so industrial nations sought colonies.
  • Colonies supplied cheap raw materials and labour, and were forced to buy finished goods.
  • Rulers monopolised trade and ignored the welfare of the colonies — e.g. India's ruined handicrafts.
questions.topperTip: Add an Indian example to any imperialism answer — it shows linkage with later chapters.

questions.question: State the positive and negative impact of imperialism.
questions.answer:
PositiveNegative
Western educationColonies = cheap raw materials
Technology — medicines, weapons, farming methodsEconomic exploitation; welfare ignored
Knowledge of new forms of governmentTrade monopolised by colonists
Nationalism and freedom strugglesRivalry led to the two World Wars

questions.question: Define: colony, protectorate, sphere of influence.
questions.answer:
• Colony: territory ruled directly by an imperial power through colonial officials.
  • Protectorate: has its own government, but its policies are guided by a foreign power (e.g. Maldives 1887–1965).
  • Sphere of influence: region where an imperial power has exclusive trading rights.
